title: India Places Largest-Ever Drone Order as Modi Pushes Indigenous Defence Tech
excerpt: The defence ministry awarded a Rs 20,000 crore contract split between Tata Advanced Systems and NIBE for 84 loitering munition systems, part of a broader push toward drone-led warfare.
body:
• India's defence ministry issued its biggest-ever single drone purchase order — 84 loitering munition systems with 840 munitions — worth part of a Rs 20,000 crore modernisation programme.
  • Tata Advanced Systems (TASL) secured 64% of the contract (54 sets, 540 munitions), while Pune-based NIBE received the remaining 36% (30 sets, 300 munitions).
  • The Indian Navy has separately begun the process to acquire ship-launched loitering munitions with a 1,000 km range and 9-hour loiter time.
  • PM Modi used his Independence Day address to call for indigenous drone and counter-drone systems and leadership in hypersonic defence technologies.

India's defence ministry has placed its largest-ever single purchase order for drones, awarding contracts for 84 sets of loitering munition systems along with 840 loiter munitions to two domestic manufacturers under the fast-track procurement procedure.

A Record Order for Indigenous Systems

The order, issued on August 14, forms part of the Indian military's broader modernisation programme valued at over Rs 20,000 crore. The programme aims to induct advanced indigenous loitering munitions, surveillance systems, and high-altitude unmanned aerial platforms from domestic firms as India shifts toward drone-led, network-centric warfare.

Tata Advanced Systems Ltd (TASL) secured the larger share — 54 sets of munition systems with 540 loitering munitions, representing 64% of the order. Pune-headquartered NIBE received the remaining 36%, covering 30 sets with 300 munitions.

"In India, sophisticated drone technology is normally imported and then mass-produced here. TASL has designed, developed and manufactured this advanced loitering munition system within the Indian ecosystem."

— Sukaran Singh, CEO & MD, Tata Advanced Systems

A loitering munition system flies to a target area, loiters to search for enemies, and then crashes into the target like a missile. The technology has gained strategic urgency following its extensive use in the Ukraine-Russia and Iran-US conflicts, and lessons from India's clash with Pakistan last year.

Modi's Independence Day Push

The contract came a day before PM Narendra Modi, in his Independence Day speech on August 15, stressed that India must develop indigenous drone and counter-drone systems and take leadership in hypersonic defence technologies. The statement underscored the government's broader Aatmanirbhar Bharat (self-reliant India) push in defence manufacturing.

TASL's system was designed entirely within the Indian ecosystem, moving from battery power to internal combustion engine technology to support larger warheads, longer endurance, and greater range. The company is also separately developing systems with a 400 km range. Its loitering munition has cleared the Army's rigorous high-altitude tests, including trials in Siachen.

NIBE's Vayu Astra-1, meanwhile, was developed after technology transfer from Israel and has been validated through high-altitude and desert trials before the company secured the contract.

Navy Joins the Drone Push

Beyond the Army, the Indian Navy has also initiated the process to acquire medium-range loitering munitions capable of ship-based operations. A request for information issued by the defence ministry seeks details of a ship-launched system with a minimum 1,000 km range, 9-hour loiter time, and a flight altitude of 15,000 feet. The system must feature electro-optical and infrared seekers for day-and-night operations with its own power supply.

What's Next

India is rapidly arming all three wings of its military with advanced drones to maintain a technology edge. The Rs 20,000 crore programme covers not just loitering munitions but also surveillance systems and high-altitude unmanned platforms. With TASL developing longer-range 400 km systems and the Navy entering the procurement cycle, the scale of India's indigenous drone ambitions is set to expand significantly in the coming months.
